newsitem.title: USA: Ford unveils alternative vehicle program.
newsitem.headline: Ford unveils alternative vehicle program.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. said Monday it hopes to perfect an alternative-fuel vehicle by the middle of the next decade that would cost no more than a mid-size sedan.

Called the P2000 and costing $150 million to $200 million to develop, the vehicle features an aluminum body and experimental aluminum-based engine. The P2000 gets its name from the fact that it weighs about 2000 pounds -- 40 percent less than a 1997 Taurus GL sedan.

At 113 cubic feet of interior passenger and luggage space, the vehicle will meet federal guidelines for a mid-sized car. It is expected to qualify as an ultra-low emissions vehicle and get up to three times the fuel economy of the current family car.
Company officials stressed at a news conference at Ford's research laboratory that the vehicle was designed to be something average car buyers could purchase.

"Our programme is aimed at a high volume vehicle -- it is a Taurus-type vehicle," said Bob Mull, Ford's director of the Partnership for a New Generation of Vehicles, a joint venture between the federal government and Detroit's Big Three automakers.
The biggest challenge remains high costs, Mull said. If the P2000 was on sale today, it would cost "many thousands of dollars" above the approximate $20,000 a Taurus GL costs now.
Funding for the P2000 has come from Ford and the federal government, with Ford contributing more than half, he said.

Ford is still experimenting with the vehicle's engine. The powertrain combines an automated version of a five-speed manual tranmission with a new direct injection aluminum, or Diata, engine that ignites with high heat instead of a spark plug.
Ford's Diata system, which runs on diesel fuel, is a four-cylinder, 1.2-litre engine that generates comparable performance to the 3.0-litre engine in the current Taurus.
To increase fuel efficiency, Ford plans to continue developing two different types of hybrid configurations that incorporate electric energy into the vehicle's propulsion system.
By the fall Ford plans to have 12 to 16 driveable prototypes. In 1998, it plans to have fully functional vehicles that meet current expectations for performance, safety, comfort and convenience.

The P2000 is the most aggressive mass market alternative fuel programme unveiled yet by one of Detroit's Big Three. Chrysler Corp. said in January it was developing a gasoline-powered "fuel cell" programme that could be commercially viable by 2010 or 2015.
General Motors Corp. last September began selling the EV1 electric car but has said it could be years before the car becomes practical for a most consumers.
